passages.text: SOUND, in philosophy, a perception of the mind, communicated by means of the ear; or that tremulous motion of the air which, being excited by the vibrations of a sounding body, is conveyed to the organ of hearing.

That air is the common medium of sound appears from the experiment of a bell rung in the receiver of an air-pump, which, as the air is exhausted, is heard fainter and fainter, till at last it can scarce be heard at all.

Some philosophers have held that sound is propagated by particles of air thrown off from the sounding body and flying to the ear. M. de Mairan supposes the air to consist of particles of different elasticities, each of which conveys one particular tone.
The velocity of sound, by the experiments of Dr Derham, is about 1142 feet in a second; and all sounds, whether loud or soft, grave or acute, move with the same velocity.

Sir Isaac Newton computed this velocity from the elasticity and density of the air, and found it about 968 feet in a second; the cause of the difference between his computation and experiment has not yet been satisfactorily explained.
Water and solid bodies convey sound better than air; for a stroke under water is heard at a great distance, and the scratch of a pin at one end of a long beam is heard at the other.
The tone of a sound, whether grave or acute, depends on the number of vibrations made in a given time by the sounding body.

In physics, sound is a vibration that travels as an acoustic wave through a medium such as a gas, liquid or solid. In human physiology, sound is the reception of such waves and their perception by the brain.
Sound needs a medium to travel. It cannot travel through a vacuum, because there is no matter there to carry the vibration.
The particles of the medium do not travel with the sound. Each particle vibrates about its resting place and passes the motion to its neighbours.

The speed of sound in dry air at 20 C is about 343 metres per second, or about 1,125 feet per second. The speed depends on the temperature. Ordinary sounds of all pitches and loudness travel at nearly the same speed in air.
Newton's calculation of the speed of sound in air gave a value that was too low. Laplace later corrected it by taking into account the heat produced when air is compressed.
Sound travels faster in liquids and solids than in air. Its speed is about 1,480 metres per second in water and about 5,960 metres per second in steel.
Pitch depends mainly on the frequency of the sound wave, that is the number of vibrations per second.
Humans can usually hear sounds with frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sound above this range is called ultrasound, and sound below it is called infrasound.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: vibration, vacuum, velocity in feet per second, Newton's computation.
Speed of sound scores well but covers only one part of the entry.

alignments.label: A vibration of the air

britannica.quote: that tremulous motion of the air

wikipedia.quote: a vibration that travels as an acoustic wave through a medium

alignments.note: Same idea in new words. Wikipedia adds that liquids and solids also carry the wave.

alignments.label: Bell in a vacuum

britannica.quote: is heard fainter and fainter, till at last it can scarce be heard at all

wikipedia.quote: It cannot travel through a vacuum

alignments.note: The air-pump experiment holds. Some sound still reaches the ear through the glass and the frame of the pump.

alignments.label: Flying particles

britannica.quote: propagated by particles of air thrown off from the sounding body and flying to the ear

wikipedia.quote: The particles of the medium do not travel with the sound

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. Only the vibration moves from the source to the ear; the air stays in place.

alignments.label: A particle for each tone

britannica.quote: each of which conveys one particular tone

wikipedia.quote: Pitch depends mainly on the frequency of the sound wave

alignments.note: The same air carries all tones. The tone depends on the frequency, as the entry itself says in B7.

alignments.label: Speed of sound
alignments.note: Close to the modern figure. The entry does not say that the speed changes with temperature.

alignments.label: Same speed for all sounds

britannica.quote: all sounds, whether loud or soft, grave or acute, move with the same velocity

wikipedia.quote: Ordinary sounds of all pitches and loudness travel at nearly the same speed in air

alignments.note: This holds for ordinary sounds. Inference: the word nearly in the modern text allows for very strong blasts.

alignments.label: Newton's computation

britannica.quote: the cause of the difference between his computation and experiment has not yet been satisfactorily explained

wikipedia.quote: Laplace later corrected it by taking into account the heat produced when air is compressed

alignments.note: The gap between theory and experiment was real in 1797. Laplace explained it after this edition.

alignments.label: Water and solids

britannica.quote: Water and solid bodies convey sound better than air

wikipedia.quote: Sound travels faster in liquids and solids than in air

alignments.note: The fact holds. Wikipedia gives the speeds in water and steel.

alignments.label: Range of hearing

wikipedia.quote: Humans can usually hear sounds with frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz

alignments.note: The 1797 entry gives no limits of hearing. Ultrasound and infrasound are later terms.

suggestedQuestions: How fast did the 1797 entry say sound travels?
How did the 1797 entry show that sound needs air?
Which 1797 ideas about how sound travels were wrong?

How fast did the 1797 entry say sound tr.answer: About 1142 feet in a second, from Derham's experiments [B4]. Wikipedia gives about 1,125 feet per second in dry air at 20 C, and says the speed depends on the temperature [W4]. The 1797 entry also noted that Newton's computed value was too low [B5], which Laplace later explained [W5].

How did the 1797 entry show that sound n.answer: With a bell rung inside the receiver of an air-pump: as the air was pumped out, the bell grew fainter until it could scarcely be heard [B2]. Wikipedia agrees that sound cannot travel through a vacuum [W2].

Which 1797 ideas about how sound travels.answer: Two reported ideas were wrong. One was that particles of air fly from the sounding body to the ear [B3]; Wikipedia says the particles only vibrate in place [W3]. The other was Mairan's idea of separate particles for each tone [B3]; pitch depends on frequency [W7].
